question: For an AC induction motor or generator, ATS 7.15.1 says the polarization index shall not be less than:
explanation: 7.15.1.D.2 sets PI not less than 2.0 and DAR not less than 1.4 for those machines. The 1.0 floor is the liquid-filled transformer rule in 7.2.2.D.2, not the motor rule. 5 MΩ is a Table 100.11 resistance, not a PI.

question: On that same AC induction-machine section, the dielectric absorption ratio shall not be less than:
explanation: ATS 7.15.1.D.2.2: DAR not less than 1.4. A generator section elsewhere (7.22.1) uses DAR greater than 1.0, so read the section that matches the machine. Do not borrow the transformer PI number.

question: An AC induction machine is larger than 200 hp. ATS 7.15.1.B.2 calls for:
choices: A one-minute test and a 60/30 DAR
A ten-minute test and a polarization index
A spot reading only, with no ratio
A DC hipot instead of insulation resistance
explanation: Above 200 hp (150 kW) the test runs ten minutes and you calculate PI. At 200 hp and less, the test is one minute and the DAR uses the 60-second and 30-second readings.

question: You want to compare a switchgear insulation reading with Table 100.1. What has to happen first?
choices: Nothing; Table 100.1 is already corrected for any temperature
Correct the reading to 20 °C with Table 100.14.1 before you compare
Correct it to 40 °C with Table 100.14.2, the rotating-machine table
Double the test voltage and ignore temperature
explanation: Table 100.1 minimums are at 20 °C, and the notes send you to Table 100.14. Correct the reading to 20 °C with Table 100.14.1 before you compare. Table 100.14.2 is the 40 °C multiplier table that sits with the machine limits in Table 100.11. Its own column labels name other apparatus, so calling it the machine table is the way the two tables are used together, not a label printed on 100.14.2. Comparing a hot raw reading with the 20 °C floor fails good insulation or passes bad insulation.

question: Table 100.11, one minute at 40 °C: the recommended minimum for AC form-wound windings built after 1970 is:
choices: kV + 1 MΩ
5 MΩ
100 MΩ
explanation: The after-1970 form-wound column is 100 MΩ across the voltage rows in that table. Random-wound stators and form-wound coils below 1 kV are 5 MΩ. kV + 1 is the column for older windings, fields, and others not listed in the modern columns.

question: A PI of 1.2 is reported. Which conclusion matches the ATS sections?
choices: Fail both a large motor and a liquid-filled transformer
It meets the liquid-filled transformer minimum of 1.0 and it does not meet the AC induction-machine minimum of 2.0
It meets the motor rule and fails the transformer rule
PI limits are identical for every apparatus in ATS
explanation: 7.2.2.D.2: transformer PI not less than 1.0. 7.15.1.D.2: machine PI not less than 2.0. Use the section for the equipment. A single 'NETA PI' does not exist.

question: You are correcting a stator insulation reading for comparison with Table 100.11. Which conversion table applies?
choices: Table 100.14.1, to 20 °C
Table 100.14.2, to 40 °C
No correction; machine readings are temperature-proof
The copper 234.5 formula, because it is a winding
explanation: Table 100.11 is the one-minute machine table at 40 °C and points at Table 100.14. Use Table 100.14.2 for that 40 °C correction. Table 100.14.1 corrects to 20 °C for the apparatus tables. The column headings on 100.14.2 name other apparatus, so the machine use follows the 40 °C pointer in Table 100.11. The copper formula corrects conductor resistance, not megohms.

question: The guard terminal on a megohmmeter is used to:
choices: Raise the test voltage
Keep surface leakage from being counted as insulation current
Discharge the winding faster than the negative lead
Measure power factor
explanation: Surface current is diverted to the guard so it does not pass through the meter’s measuring circuit. It does not raise the voltage and it does not replace a clean, dry surface. The Megger S1-568 manual describes the guard for that leakage path.
reference: Megger S1-568 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: A megohmmeter voltage lock (a ceiling you set and the set will not exceed) is for:
choices: Making every test 15 kV
Keeping the applied voltage inside what the insulation is allowed to see
Replacing the temperature correction
Skipping the discharge
explanation: The S1-568 manual gives XLPE cable that should not be tested above 5000 V as the example of why a lock exists. The right voltage still comes from the equipment rating or the ATS table, not from the highest range on the dial.
reference: Megger S1-568 user manual, per manufacturer instructions; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.1 for the voltage when the manufacturer is silent

question: After a megohmmeter test the winding is:
choices: Left charged so the next reading is faster
Discharged through the set before the leads come off and before anyone touches it
Shorted with bare hands
Fine to handle because DC insulation tests have no stored energy
explanation: The specimen is a capacitor. The S1-568 and every other serious megohmmeter discharge at the end of the test. Pulling the leads first is how people get hit. ATS machine and transformer procedures assume you do not leave the winding hot.
reference: Megger S1-568 user manual, per manufacturer instructions (test completion and discharge)

question: ATS Table 100.11 gives rotating-machine insulation resistance for a one-minute test at 40 °C. That minimum is applied:
choices: Raw, at whatever temperature you found
After correction to 40 °C
After correction to 75 °C with the copper constant
Only if the PI is above 4
explanation: ATS Table 100.11 is a one-minute value at 40 °C. IEEE 43-2013 clause 12.3 and Table 4 use the same temperature: correct the reading to 40 °C before comparing it with the minimum. The 20 °C multipliers in ATS Table 100.14.1 belong to the apparatus in Table 100.1, not to this machine table.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.11 and 7.15.1.D.2; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clause 12.3 and Table 4

question: PI on a machine whose 1-minute reading is 8000 MΩ should be:
choices: Failed if it is under 4
Not used as the pass/fail, because IEEE 43 does not recommend PI once the 1-minute value is above 5000 MΩ
Doubled and compared with Table 100.1
Run at twice the test voltage
explanation: 8000 megohms is above the 5000 megohm line in IEEE 43-2013 clause 12.2.2, so the polarization index is not the pass/fail. Clause 11.2 says it may be disregarded. The machine still has to meet the insulation-resistance minimum in ATS Table 100.11, corrected to 40 °C. A PI under 2.0 is the ATS floor only when the index is actually being used.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.15.1.D.2 and Table 100.11; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clauses 11.2 and 12.2.2

question: The guard terminal on a megohmmeter is connected so that:
choices: Surface leakage is kept out of the measured current
The test voltage doubles
The winding is discharged through the operator
Power factor is calculated
explanation: Guard shunts leakage that would otherwise look like insulation current. It does not raise the voltage and it does not replace a clean surface. The Megger S1-568 manual describes that terminal, and ATS insulation tests assume you know which lead is the measurement.
reference: Megger S1-568 user manual, per manufacturer instructions; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 insulation-resistance tests

question: A transformer winding's insulation resistance to ground reads close to zero. That points to a grounded winding, a winding-to-winding short, or heavy carbon tracking. What should you do next?
choices: Accept it if the oil is new
Retest at a higher voltage until it reads higher
Correct it to 20 °C, and it will pass
Confirm with other tests, such as polarization index, insulation power factor, or moisture in the insulating liquid
explanation: A very low reading is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Back it up with PI, power factor, and liquid moisture before deciding. For normal readings, comparison with factory or earlier results means more than the absolute number of megohms. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.2 and D.2; ref. IEEE C57.152-2025, 7.2.13.4.

question: A natural-ester-filled transformer reads lower insulation resistance than a similar mineral-oil unit. How should you read that?
choices: Ester units must meet the same absolute megohm value as mineral oil
Low insulation resistance in an ester unit always means water in the paper
This is generally expected for ester-filled units. Judge it against that unit's own factory and earlier results
Insulation resistance cannot be measured on ester units
explanation: The guide notes that ester-filled transformers generally have lower insulation resistance than mineral-oil units, and that higher temperature lowers readings too. The most useful comparison is with factory and earlier results.

question: During a stepped dc insulation-resistance test on a transformer winding, the current starts climbing without leveling off. The guides say to:
choices: Raise the voltage to the next step to see if it stabilizes
Hold for 10 minutes to get a PI
Switch to a lower-range megohmmeter and continue
Stop the test immediately
explanation: Current that keeps rising at constant voltage points to insulation heading toward breakdown. The test codes say to stop at once. Afterward, ground the terminals long enough for trapped charge to bleed off.

question: Above what 1-minute insulation-resistance reading should the polarization index stop being used to judge a machine winding?
choices: 5 MΩ
100 MΩ
1 Ω
explanation: Clause 12.2.2 says that once the 1-minute value is higher than 5000 megohms, the current is so small that humidity, voltage drift, and the leads can move the 10-minute ratio. The index may or may not describe the insulation, so it is not used as the assessment. Clause 11.2 says the same thing: the index can be disregarded. ATS 7.15.1.B.2 still runs the test in accordance with IEEE 43, and 7.15.1.D.2.1 still prints a PI floor of 2.0 when the index is used.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.15.1.B.2 and D.2.1; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clauses 11.2 and 12.2.2

question: For rotating-machine windings built before 1970, ATS Table 100.11’s recommended minimum insulation resistance is:
choices: kV + 1 megohms, not the flat 100 megohm column used for later form-wound windings
Always 100 megohms
Always 5 ohms
The control-wiring floor of 2 megohms
explanation: The older-winding column, and field windings, use kV + 1. A 4 kV machine in that column is about 5 megohms, not 100. Form-wound windings built after 1970 use the 100 megohm column. The whole table is a one-minute value at 40 °C.

question: ATS Table 100.11 lists the DC test voltage for machine windings rated under 1000 V as:
choices: 10 kV
explanation: Under 1000 V, the table’s DC test voltage is 500 V. The minimum resistance still depends on which column the winding belongs in, and the value is for one minute at 40 °C. Do not grab the 5 kV or 10 kV megohmmeter range because it is on the dial.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.11; test method ref. IEEE 43 per 7.15.1.B.2

question: In ATS Table 100.11, random-wound stator coils and form-wound coils below 1 kV have a recommended minimum of:
choices: 5 megohms
100 megohms
kV + 1, with no other column
2 megohms, the control-wire floor
explanation: That column is 5 megohms. The 100 megohm column is the later form-wound winding above that description. Control wiring at 2 megohms is a switchgear rule, not this machine cell. Correct the reading to 40 °C first.

question: Unless another pair of times is stated, the polarization index on a machine winding is:
choices: The 1-minute resistance divided by the 10-minute resistance
The 10-minute resistance divided by the 1-minute resistance
The 30-second resistance divided by the 1-minute resistance
A spot reading at 1 minute only
explanation: The index is the 10-minute value over the 1-minute value. Inverting it makes a healthy winding look bad. ATS 7.15.1.B.2 uses that 10-minute test on machines larger than 200 horsepower. Smaller machines in that section use the 60/30 ratio instead.

question: ATS sends you to Table 100.11 for a machine winding rated under 1000 V. The dc insulation-resistance test voltage is:
choices: 500 V dc
2500 V dc
10 kV dc
The highest range on the megohmmeter
explanation: Clause 5.3 and Table 1 put windings at or under 1000 V on a 500 V direct test. ATS Table 100.11 uses that same 500 V step. A higher range can overstress a small or wet winding. The reading is still corrected to 40 °C before it is compared.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.11 and 7.15.1.B.2; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clause 5.3 and Table 1

question: Evaluating a motor PI under ATS 7.15.1, what minimum polarization index applies to thermal class 105 (class A) insulation?
choices: 2.0, the same number it uses for class 130 and above
explanation: Class 105 is 1.5. Class 130 and above is 2.0. ATS 7.15.1.D.2.1 prints a single floor of 2.0 for the AC machines in that section, which is the higher of those two IEEE floors. Do not use 1.5 to pass a machine that ATS holds to 2.0, and do not quote 2.0 as the IEEE floor for class A.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.15.1.D.2.1; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clause 12.2 and Table 3

question: On a motor, you test one phase with the other two grounded instead of all three together. Compared with the whole-winding reading, the one-phase reading can be:
choices: Exactly three times the whole-winding value, always
Lower than three times the whole-winding value, because of phase-to-phase current
Higher than the Table 4 minimum with no correction
Independent of temperature
explanation: Current between phases adds to the reading, so one phase can look worse than a simple three-times rule. The value you compare is still the observed resistance corrected to 40 °C. ATS Table 100.11 is that 40 °C table.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.11; ref. IEEE 43-2013, clause 12.3
